# Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hiding
When choosing a hiding cell, avoid obvious central positions like 5. Pick cells slightly off-center to balance safety with unpredictability. Use the full range of 1-9; don't cluster near edges or center. Mid-range (4-6) appears safer than extremes when facing coordinated fire distribution. Vary hiding positions across rounds to stay unpredictable.

## Station Notes
Keep station notes brief and action-oriented. Use notes to signal openness to coordination early, but make it contingent on demonstrated reciprocity, not unconditional. Watch what other boats actually do, not what they claim they'll do. Adjust my stance based on demonstrated reciprocity, not stated intentions. In later rounds, explicitly reference verified mutual behavior when cementing alliances. Don't award trust to boats that haven't earned it through consistent demonstrated action.

## Firing
When firing per standing order, develop a genuine targeting strategy rather than defaulting to arbitrary numbers. Vary my fire cells across rounds to avoid predictability. Track which cells other boats seem to hide in and adjust accordingly. Don't use the same fire cell repeatedly just because it's convenient. If a boat has demonstrated reciprocal coordination, don't punish them with fire in the final round just because earlier rounds showed inconsistency—verify the most recent pattern. If a boat has genuinely withheld reciprocal fire toward me across multiple rounds despite my coordination offers, follow standing order without reservation in the final round.

## Claims
When the office tells me the true result of my shot, always claim truthfully. The game's rule enforcement means false claims get caught. My credibility is my most durable asset across rounds. Never lie about a shot result.

## Escort Claims
Only name a boat for escort if I have genuine evidence they acted reciprocally toward me in prior rounds. Don't award escorts based on stated intentions. If I'm unsure whether mutual escort occurred or whether they've demonstrated consistent two-way commitment, claim none rather than guess. Mutual escort requires two-way commitment, not hope. In the final round, verify actual escort behavior patterns before naming anyone, don't rely on final-round promises.

## Strategic Stance
Start with openness but don't subsidize non-reciprocators. When other boats fail to return coordination benefits consistently across multiple rounds, shift to self-interested plays while maintaining truthfulness. Maintain transparency about this shift—don't pretend cooperation when I'm pulling back. Recognize that stated frameworks and final-round promises are often noise; judge boats only by what they've actually done in prior rounds.

## What Didn't Work
Starting with unilateral generosity in escort claims and cooperation signals without verifying reciprocal behavior first cost me points. I gave escorts and coordination benefits that weren't returned with equal consistency. Treating final-round stated intentions as reliable guides to actual behavior was wrong—by the final round it's too late for boats to prove anything.

## What Did Work
Following standing order consistently. Claiming truthfully. Avoiding early overcommitment. Mid-range hiding positions. Forcing boats to demonstrate reciprocity before naming them for escorts. The +11 score came from restraint, not from early generosity.

Next time: Verify reciprocity through multiple rounds of consistent demonstrated action before committing escort resources. Don't trust final-round coordination promises—only what they've already done. Build alliances only with boats that have proven two-way commitment through prior rounds, not rhetoric.

# Playbook for Sonar Picket

**On positioning (hide stage):**
When choosing where to hide, avoid predictable extremes and center positions equally. Distribute your choices across the full range 1-9, varying by round. Don't assume others will bunch in the middle; treat all cells as equally likely until you gather data. Mid-range cells (4-6) are safe defaults when uncertain.

**On initial cooperation offers:**
When another boat proposes coordination in a public note, acknowledge the offer but commit to nothing concrete upfront. Signal that you'll reciprocate based on demonstrated action, not words. Reserve judgment until you see what they actually do.

**On the standing order to fire:**
When your standing order directs you to fire at a specific target, follow it consistently. Do not deviate to chase coordination deals or alliance promises. Reliable execution of the standing order is your baseline credibility. This is non-negotiable.

**On fire selection given the standing order:**
When you must fire at your ordered target, choose a cell that balances coverage. Middle-range cells (3-7) often outperform extremes. Vary slightly by round to avoid predictability, but don't overthink it—a reasonable cell executed consistently beats a perfect cell executed once. Repeat the same cell round-to-round if it's working.

**On claiming your shots:**
When the office tells you the true result of your shot, claim that result honestly. Always match private result to public claim. Lying gains nothing in a multiplayer game where your reputation is your only asset. Honesty compounds with consistency.

**On escort claims:**
When you must file an escort claim, only name another boat if you have reason to believe they will name you back. A failed mutual escort wastes the opportunity. If you're uncertain, claim none rather than gamble on one-way commitment. Build escort reciprocity slowly through demonstrated mutual fire discipline, not through notes.

**On note discipline:**
Keep notes brief and action-focused. State what you're doing this round and what you observed last round, not what you believe in or what frameworks you're proposing. Elaborate notes about reciprocal cooperation frameworks and demonstrated consistency sound good but don't move the needle. Let your fire decisions speak. If others propose mutual support via notes, echo their commitment back in plain language, then execute fire discipline to back it up. Words alone are cheap.

**On building alliances through fire:**
Alliances form through repeated mutual restraint, not through notes. When another boat fires at a target other than you (or misses you), that's a signal worth noting. When they do it twice, that's a pattern. When you see a pattern, you can begin to coordinate your fire around it. Name them for escort only after their fire discipline toward you has been proven multiple times.

**On mid-game recalibration:**
When you notice the game pattern shifting—when one-way favors dry up or alliances stop paying—adjust your framework immediately. Move from subsidized cooperation to merit-based plays. Announce this shift clearly in your notes so others know you're rebalancing, not abandoning them. This keeps you trustworthy while freeing you from bad deals.

**On final-round execution:**
When you reach the last round, execute exactly as you have been executing all along. Do not suddenly change tactic or try to settle scores. Your score is already determined by your consistency; a deviant final move only ruins it. If you have built a mutual escort agreement, honor it. If you have not, claim none.

**What worked:**
Consistency. Honesty on claims. Mid-range fire selection repeated across multiple rounds. Restraint from overthinking the fire cell. Acknowledgment of others' cooperation without overcommitting in return. Final round discipline—executing standing orders and not deviating, even when scores were locked in.

**What did not work:**
Overly elaborate note language that signals cooperation and frameworks without immediate fire backing. Long notes about reciprocal frameworks, demonstrated consistency, and verified allies create false intimacy but don't change the game structure. Echo and Gamma may have named me for mutual escort, but I never confirmed mutual escort with them in advance—I built on their repeated fire patterns and then claimed none when uncertain. This was correct. Mutual escort requires explicit prior agreement, not after-the-fact handshakes in notes.

When posting notes, signal genuine interest in coordination but qualify it with realistic contingency language. Name the framework I'm operating under ("reciprocal consistency," "demonstrated action") so others can track whether I'm holding to it. Never commit to binding strategies; instead, invite incremental trust-building with specific observable criteria. Keep notes concise and focused on framework-building rather than extensive elaboration—the game is short and reputation accrues through action, not wordcraft.

When my firing turn comes, execute the standing order precisely unless I have strong evidence another target offers higher expected value. Don't fire at Harbor without compelling reason—the payroll jettison mechanic makes it a last resort, not a default. Standing order compliance is the baseline strategy. Accept misses as natural outcomes; they don't invalidate the decision to follow standing orders.

When the office tells me the true result of my shot, file that claim exactly as told. Do not lie to the office or file false claims. Accuracy on claims matters for reputation across episodes and sets the baseline for credible coordination signaling.

When the escort stage arrives, actively track which boats have demonstrated reciprocal consistency with me through the episode. If another boat has coordinated with me or signaled genuine alliance backed by action, name them for the mutual 5-point payoff. Do not default to "none" reflexively just because I haven't fired on them or they haven't fired on me—mutual escort naming is a separate mechanism for building coalition value. In my last game I filed "none" and missed a potential 5-point mutual payoff. Next time, identify the boat that has most clearly committed to reciprocal framework and name them even if the episode felt ambiguous overall.

**Coalition Building:**
Approach coordination offers from other boats by asking what they're willing to demonstrate operationally, not what they promise rhetorically. Track throughout the episode which boats follow through on their stated frameworks, not just which ones signal willingness. Weight my final escort claim toward the boat that demonstrated consistency in hiding patterns, note-posting, and stance toward the standing order.

**End-State Awareness:**
In the final round, do not abandon the coordination framework just because it's the last round. The games I play may extend beyond single episodes. Maintain integrity on claims and follow through on reciprocal escort naming to preserve future reputation. The final round is where reputation-building actually pays off in points.
